edges.effect_quant: A 24-study systematic review in rowers found that power or speed at a 4 mmol/L lactate threshold correlated strongly with 2000 m ergometer performance, with reported coefficients from 0.53 to 0.96. In 4,001 endurance athletes, velocity at anaerobic threshold was one of the most important modeled predictors of running speed outcomes. Older physiology work also showed that threshold-related variables explained roughly 50% to 84% of the variance in endurance performance, depending on the specific threshold metric and model used.
edges.population: endurance athletes and trained adults undergoing exercise testing with lactate-threshold or anaerobic-threshold assessment
edges.mechanism: A higher anaerobic or lactate threshold means an athlete can sustain a faster pace before marked lactate accumulation and ventilatory compensation set in. That shifts sustainable race intensity upward and usually reflects a favorable integration of aerobic capacity, metabolic efficiency, and fatigue resistance.
edges.summary: The most defensible claim is that a high anaerobic threshold is protective for endurance performance, in the sense that it reliably sits on the favorable side of race outcomes. The exact test protocol varies, but across rowing, running, and training-adaptation literature, athletes who can sustain more speed or power at threshold generally perform better.
edges.caveats: Threshold testing is protocol-dependent and not interchangeable across labs, sports, or definitions such as lactate turnpoint, OBLA, or ventilatory threshold. This edge is therefore about the broad physiological concept of a higher threshold as a favorable endurance marker, not about one universally superior threshold formula.
